publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: In conclusion, taken together, these results provide compelling evidence for autonomous syntax: The production of a sentence critically depends upon an abstract syntactic form that is defined in terms of part-of-speech forms (e.g., nouns, verbs, prepositions) and phrasal constituents organized from those (noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases), and this abstract syntactic form has a large influence upon structural priming.

span.label: structural priming
span.quote: When people talk or write, they tend to repeat the underlying basic structures that they recently produced or experienced others produce.

span.label: review
span.quote: In short, structural priming is an informative and heavily investigated phenomenon and therefore warrants an extensive and directed review.

span.label: Residual activation (the one-locus account): using a construction leaves its combinatorial node and the lemma linked to it partly activated, so the same structure is cheaper to produce for a while. The lexical boost falls out of the same machinery - a repeated verb re-activates both the lemma AND the strengthened link to the node - which is what makes it ONE locus.
span.quote: On this account, priming is due to residual activation of combinatorial and lemma nodes, as well as the links between the two (as illustrated in Panel C of Figure 2 ). More specifically, lexically independent priming occurs as a result of the residual activation

span.label: Implicit learning: producing or understanding a structure requires having learned how meaning relationships map onto functional elements and onto constituent order, and every sentence experienced re-weights those mappings. On this account priming is not a trace that decays but the visible edge of the same learning that acquired the grammar.
span.quote: The core idea is that for people to produce and comprehend language, they must learn how their different linguistic and language-related representations relate or map onto one other. To produce or understand the word cat , a language user must learn that the meaning of domestic feline maps onto the word cat (which is a noun), which in turn maps onto the sound sequence /kæt/ and so forth. Everyday language experience can drive the learning of this knowledge

span.label: Observing structural priming does not license the inference that abstract syntax caused it.
span.quote: However, this does not mean that whenever structural priming is observed, it is always caused by abstract syntactic knowledge.

span.label: The evidence on whether thematic roles affect priming is contradictory and unresolved by this review.
span.quote: In sum, the effects of thematic roles on priming are mixed, and more work is needed to determine how they fit into the mapping from message to syntax.

span.label: All cross-linguistic priming evidence comes from typologically and genetically related languages.
span.quote: More immediately, they provide evidence about the degree of sharing of grammar between languages, though it is important to note that all languages explored thus far (English, French, German, Dutch, Spanish, Greek) are genetically and typologically related.

span.label: Why priming in comprehension usually needs a boost cannot be decided from current evidence.
span.quote: Overall, it is unclear whether priming in comprehension generally requires a boost because priming of comprehension involve different cognitive bases than priming of production, or because priming of comprehension is typically assessed with less sensitive reaction-time measures.

span.label: priming between production and comprehension, and between writing and speaking, is read as evidence that the two processes draw on the SAME representations - a claim that carries structure across the production/comprehension divide
span.quote: Indeed, priming between production and comprehension, just like priming between writing and speaking, supports the claim that both processes draw on common representations of linguistic information, particularly ones associated with syntax.

span.label: a CONTROL EXPERIMENT in which the primes had the same noun-phrase types but were modified by ADVERBIAL clauses instead of relative clauses
span.note: eliminates: that the priming comes from the noun phrases or from lexical repetition rather than from the relative-clause structure itself
span.quote: Specifically, in a control experiment, subjects produced primes that had the same types of noun phrases, but that were modified by adverbial clauses rather than relative clauses (“the servant of the actress when she…” instead of “the servant of the actress who…”).

span.label: structural priming
span.quote: In the language sciences, a ubiquitous form of such repetition is structural priming , a tendency to repeat or better process a current sentence because of its structural similarity to a previously experienced (“prime”) sentence ( Bock, 1986 ). The recent explosion of research in structural priming has made it the dominant means of investigating the processes involved in the production (and increasingly, comprehension) of complex expressions such as sentences

span.label: repetition
span.quote: Repetition is central because it can reflect the operation of many different underlying psychological mechanisms. It can reflect learning and development (as we acquire a capability, we begin to repeat the products of that capability), imitation (we can repeat others’ behavior to accomplish social as well as learning and development goals), and (lack of) executive control (when repetitive behavior reflects a perseverative tendency and so an inability to inhibit a previous and now potent response)

span.label: lexical boost
span.quote: We refer to this as the lexical boost to structural priming. Corpus studies have also provided evidence of a lexical boost

span.label: residual activation
span.quote: On this account, priming is due to residual activation of combinatorial and lemma nodes, as well as the links between the two (as illustrated in Panel C of Figure 2 ). More specifically, lexically independent priming occurs as a result of the residual activation

span.label: implicit learning
span.quote: These findings, together with a few other properties of structural priming (noted below), has led to a view that it at least in part reflects the operation of an implicit learning mechanism. The core idea is that for people to produce and comprehend language, they must learn how their different linguistic and language-related representations relate

span.label: abstract syntactic form
span.quote: The production of a sentence critically depends upon an abstract syntactic form that is defined in terms of part-of-speech forms (e.g., nouns, verbs, prepositions) and phrasal constituents organized from those (noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases), and this abstract syntactic form has a large influence upon structural priming

span.label: syntactic priming
span.quote: Some researchers use the term syntactic priming (e.g., Pickering & Branigan, 1999 ), but we shall use structural priming because it encompasses abstract linguistic priming that need not be syntactic (e.g., Bock, Loebell, & Morey, 1992 ), and indeed does not presuppose the existence of specifically syntactic representations

span.label: dialogue
span.quote: In dialogue, interlocutors constantly switch between comprehension and production, and are clearly able to use what they have just comprehended to guide what they produce. Thus it is not surprising that dialogue is extremely repetitive

span.label: structural priming - THE LINGUISTICS SENSE, and it shares almost nothing with the social-psychology sense this corpus is otherwise full of except the word. The prime is a SENTENCE, the primed thing is its STRUCTURE, the response is another sentence, and the effect is defined disjunctively: to repeat OR BETTER PROCESS a current sentence because of its structural similarity to a previously experienced one. No concept is activated, no behaviour is influenced, no attitude is reached
span.quote: In the language sciences, a ubiquitous form of such repetition is structural priming , a tendency to repeat or better process a current sentence because of its structural similarity to a previously experienced (“prime”) sentence ( Bock, 1986 ). The recent explosion of research in structural priming has made it the dominant means of investigating the processes involved in the production (and increasingly, comprehension) of complex expressions such as sentences

span.label: structural priming versus syntactic priming - A NAME CHOSEN AGAINST A THEORY, and the clearest instance of it in this corpus. The review drops `syntactic priming` (Pickering's own term from 1999) for `structural priming` on the explicit ground that the old name PRESUPPOSES THE EXISTENCE OF SPECIFICALLY SYNTACTIC REPRESENTATIONS - the very thing the method is used to test. A term retired because it smuggles in the conclusion, with the reason stated in the sentence that retires it
span.quote: Some researchers use the term syntactic priming (e.g., Pickering & Branigan, 1999 ), but we shall use structural priming because it encompasses abstract linguistic priming that need not be syntactic (e.g., Bock, Loebell, & Morey, 1992 ), and indeed does not presuppose the existence of specifically syntactic representations

span.label: priming as a DIAGNOSTIC INSTRUMENT - the reason the field runs these experiments at all, and the review states the logic in general form before applying it: because being affected by repetition depends on how knowledge is represented, the pattern of what does and does not prime is used to READ OFF the representations. The effect is evidence about something else
span.quote: the tendency to be affected by the repetition of aspects of knowledge can be used to diagnose the nature of that knowledge. So in this case, the tendency to repeat aspects of sentence structure helps researchers identify some of the representations that people construct

span.label: USING priming versus investigating priming - the review's own closing recommendation, and it is this project's central distinction stated by the people who own the term: an investigation USING structural priming should not be cast as an investigation ABOUT structural priming, because when priming is merely a dependent variable the real subject is the representation under test. A field telling itself to keep instrument and object apart
span.quote: we feel that it is critical that investigations using structural priming should not primarily be cast as investigations about structural priming. Sometimes, structural priming is merely a dependent variable, when patterns of priming are used to infer the operation of certain kinds of representations or processes (e.g., when priming suggests the use of phrase-structure rules, or the absence of a dominance-only level of representation). In these cases, the central issue is the representational or processing feature under investigation

span.label: one-locus versus two-locus - the field's name for its own open question, and it is a question about IDENTITY rather than about size: is the lexical boost the same mechanism as abstract priming working harder, or a second mechanism altogether? The review states the test that would separate them - a dissociation the two-locus account predicts and the one-locus account does not - and does not claim to have it
span.quote: One is a two-locus account, which assumes that separate mechanisms or cognitive systems lead to abstract (lexically independent) priming and lexicalized (lexically boosted) priming. The other is a one-locus account, which assumes that a single mechanism can explain both abstract priming and the lexical boost. The two-locus account suggests that a dissociation of the two priming effects should occur under some circumstances but the one-locus account does not

span.label: priming as a METHOD, said in as many words in the review's last sentence - not a phenomenon the field studies but an instrument it expects to keep using, described by its instrumental virtues (strong, versatile, resilient) rather than by what it is
span.quote: Structural priming has proved to be a strong, versatile, and resilient phenomenon. It is informative about the mechanisms that underlie language use in many different populations, and appears to facilitate both language learning and communication. We predict that it will remain a central psycholinguistic method for many years to come

span.label: contradicts → functionalist approaches to syntactic structure (Bates & MacWhinney, 1982) and connectionist views that eschew traditional syntactic representations (McClelland, St. John, & Taraban, 1989)
span.quote: This runs against more functionalist approaches to syntactic structure (e.g., Bates & MacWhinney, 1982 ), as well as other views that eschew traditional representations of syntactic knowledge (e.g., McClelland, St. John, & Taraban, 1989 ).

span.label: contradicts → transformational accounts of syntactic production with a deep-structure level (Chomsky, 1965)
span.quote: In fact, this animacy effect disconfirms a transformational account of syntactic production.

span.label: residual activation —causes→ syntactic priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.8 — Weighted 0.8, not higher, because the review presents this as ONE OF TWO live accounts and declines to choose between them. This span is also the one-locus account's answer to the lexical boost: a repeated verb re-activates the lemma, the strengthened link AND the combinatorial node, so the bigger effect needs no second mechanism.
span.quote: But when a sentence contains the same verb as a previous sentence (e.g., give ), syntactic priming results from residual activation of the pre-activated lemma node ( give ), of the strengthened link between this lemma node and the NP,NP combinatorial node, and (as in lexically independent priming) of the combinatorial node itself

span.label: syntactic priming —same-as→ structural priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — A DELIBERATE RENAMING WITH THE REASON ATTACHED, and the discarded term is Pickering's own from 1999. The stated ground is that the old name PRESUPPOSES what the method is supposed to test - whether the primed representations are syntactic at all - so the rename is an argument, not a matter of style. Confidence 0.95: the paper states the identity itself.
span.quote: Some researchers use the term syntactic priming (e.g., Pickering & Branigan, 1999 ), but we shall use structural priming because it encompasses abstract linguistic priming that need not be syntactic (e.g., Bock, Loebell, & Morey, 1992 ), and indeed does not presuppose the existence of specifically syntactic representations

span.label: implicit learning —causes→ structural priming
span.note: direction on the measure: increases · strength of the relation: 0.8 — The rival account, at the same weight as residual activation because the review gives it the same standing. `at least in part` is the field's own hedge, and the review's summary position is that the two accounts may not be as incompatible as is usually assumed.
span.quote: These findings, together with a few other properties of structural priming (noted below), has led to a view that it at least in part reflects the operation of an implicit learning mechanism

span.label: lexical boost —part-of→ structural priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — `the lexical boost TO structural priming` - the field's own preposition makes it a component of the effect rather than a separate one. Whether it is a separate MECHANISM is exactly what one-locus / two-locus disputes, so the edge records the part relation the term commits to and nothing more.
span.quote: We refer to this as the lexical boost to structural priming. Corpus studies have also provided evidence of a lexical boost

span.label: structural priming —operationalised-as→ abstract syntactic form
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.85 — The direction that matters for this corpus: the priming effect is the MEASURING INSTRUMENT and the abstract syntactic form is what it is used to detect. Read the other way round it would say the form is the effect, which is not what the review claims.
span.quote: The production of a sentence critically depends upon an abstract syntactic form that is defined in terms of part-of-speech forms (e.g., nouns, verbs, prepositions) and phrasal constituents organized from those (noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases), and this abstract syntactic form has a large influence upon structural priming

span.label: structural priming —is-a→ repetition
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.9 — Recorded because the superordinate is chosen and not obvious: this field files priming under REPETITION - alongside imitation, perseveration and learning - rather than under activation or accessibility, which is where the social-psychology records in this corpus put it. The same word, filed under two different genera.
span.quote: In the language sciences, a ubiquitous form of such repetition is structural priming , a tendency to repeat or better process a current sentence because of its structural similarity to a previously experienced (“prime”) sentence ( Bock, 1986 ). The recent explosion of research in structural priming has made it the dominant means of investigating the processes involved in the production (and increasingly, comprehension) of complex expressions such as sentences

span.label: In a corpus of 3,003 naturally occurring prepositional-object / double-object pairs, both members used the same construction in nearly two-thirds of cases, and the tendency was significantly stronger when prime and target shared a verb - the lexical boost observed outside the laboratory, in speech nobody arranged.
span.quote: In nearly two-thirds of instances, the first and second member of the pair involved the same construction – that is, priming was observed. Interestingly, this tendency to repeat structure was significantly stronger when the prime and target used the same verb than when they did not

span.label: Abstract syntactic form - parts of speech and the phrasal constituents built from them - has a large influence on structural priming, which the review takes as the method's central evidential yield for autonomous syntax while explicitly denying that it is the only thing that primes.
span.quote: The production of a sentence critically depends upon an abstract syntactic form that is defined in terms of part-of-speech forms (e.g., nouns, verbs, prepositions) and phrasal constituents organized from those (noun phrases, verb phrases, prepositional phrases), and this abstract syntactic form has a large influence upon structural priming. This runs against more functionalist approaches to syntactic structure (e.g., Bates & MacWhinney, 1982 ), as well as other views that eschew traditional representations of syntactic knowledge (e.g., McClelland, St. John, & Taraban, 1989 ). However, this conclusion should not be taken to mean that only abstract syntactic forms cause priming. We have already suggested that most or all levels of representation may prime. In short, abstract syntax is a central but apparently not exclusive type of knowledge that causes structural priming

span.label: Repeating the verb between prime and target enhances priming, and in at least one study the effect was not significant at all without verb repetition - which is what makes the lexical boost a candidate for a second mechanism rather than a mere amplifier.
span.quote: When the verb was not repeated, this tendency was not significant, and priming was significantly stronger when the verb was repeated than when it was not

span.label: 3003 — prepositional-object / double-object sentence pairs Gries identified in a corpus of British English
span.quote: Gries (2005) identified 3003 pairs of prepositional-object and double-object constructions (which were not necessarily adjacent) in a corpus of British English

span.label: two-thirds — the share of those corpus pairs whose two members used the same construction - priming visible in unarranged speech
span.quote: In nearly two-thirds of instances, the first and second member of the pair involved the same construction – that is, priming was observed
